title: Completing the Square to Identify an Implicit Circle
originalTopic: Implicit equations and completing the square
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: An implicit-plotting command draws a closed curve for x^2 + y^2 = 4x + 4y - 4, but the software reports no center or radius. Rewrite the equation in standard form and state the center, the radius, and a suitable window.

steps.title: Collect the variable terms
steps.explanation: Moving the linear terms to the left leaves the constant on the right and groups the x's and y's for completing the square.
steps.why: The general second-degree form with equal x^2 and y^2 coefficients and no xy term is a circle only after the squares are isolated.

steps.title: Complete both squares
steps.explanation: Adding 4 and 4 to both sides balances the two completed squares, producing the standard circle equation with right-hand side 2 squared.
steps.why: Whatever is added inside a square must also be added to the other side, otherwise the equation changes its solution set.

steps.title: Read off center and radius
steps.explanation: Comparing with (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2 gives h = 2, k = 2, r = 2, so the circle is tangent to both coordinate axes.
steps.why: Tangency to the axes is a checkable geometric consequence, confirming that the radius really is 2.

steps.title: Choose an equal-scale window
steps.explanation: With a 1:1 aspect ratio and just a half-unit margin outside the circle's bounding box, the implicit plot renders as a true circle rather than an ellipse.
steps.why: Implicit plots are especially sensitive to unequal scaling, since there is no explicit function to resample and correct the distortion.
